source_caption:
Jean-Luc Godard’s Pierrot le Fou (1965) turns every frame into a painting.

Blending bold primary colors, pop art influences, and unconventional camerawork, Godard rejected traditional filmmaking in favor of something more expressive and unpredictable. Rather than simply telling a story, the film captures emotion through color, composition, and movement, making each scene feel like a work of art.

More than sixty years later, Pierrot le Fou remains one of the defining films of the French New Wave and a lasting influence on cinema, fashion, and visual culture.
